pages.description: Install and operate the Data Hub watcher as a Windows service so it starts on boot, survives logouts, and can auto-update in the background.
pages.markdown:
# Run as a Windows service (/docs/windows-service)



**For:** Lab operators

On a lab instrument PC, run the watcher as a Windows service. This is the default setup: the service starts on boot, keeps running after you log out, restarts on failure, and participates in [fleet auto-update](/docs/watcher-releases). Foreground `data-hub-watcher watch` is for quick checks and non-Windows hosts.

## Install the service extra [#install-the-service-extra]

The service depends on `pywin32`, which ships in the `windows-service` extra. The [default install](/docs/install-the-watcher#install) already includes it. If you installed without it, add it now:

```sh
uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

Run [`data-hub-watcher init`](/docs/install-the-watcher#configure) first if you have not configured the watcher yet. The service uses the same `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` and per-environment `.env` file.

## Install and start [#install-and-start]

From an **Administrator** terminal:

```sh
data-hub-watcher service install
data-hub-watcher service start
```

`service install` registers delayed auto-start (so it does not race the network stack at boot), configures restart-on-failure recovery, and registers the `DataHubWatcherUpgrade` Scheduled Task used by the auto-updater.

<Callout type="warn">
  The Windows auto-update path requires that `service install` (or `service reinstall`) has been run from an Administrator shell at least once. Fleet PCs upgrading into an auto-update-capable build for the first time need a one-time `service reinstall` to pick up the task.
</Callout>

## Lifecycle commands [#lifecycle-commands]

| Command                              | What it does                                  |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `data-hub-watcher service install`   | Register the service                          |
| `data-hub-watcher service start`     | Start the service                             |
| `data-hub-watcher service stop`      | Stop the service                              |
| `data-hub-watcher service status`    | Show whether the service is running           |
| `data-hub-watcher service uninstall` | Remove the service                            |
| `data-hub-watcher service reinstall` | Stop, uninstall, install, and start in one go |

`service reinstall` is the right command after an out-of-band wheel swap (for example a manual `uv tool install -U` from an Administrator shell). Stop and uninstall are best-effort, so it works even if the service is already gone.

`service install` and `service reinstall` accept `--env-path PATH` to override which `.env` file the service loads (defaults to `~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>`).

## Do not run `watch` alongside the service [#do-not-run-watch-alongside-the-service]

Running `data-hub-watcher watch` interactively while the service is also running is not supported: both processes would race on the same log file and watch directory. Stop the service first if you need the CLI for debugging:

```powershell
data-hub-watcher service stop
data-hub-watcher --verbose watch
data-hub-watcher service start
```

## Where the service writes logs [#where-the-service-writes-logs]

The service and the CLI share one rotating log:

* `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log`

A separate `service-bootstrap.log` next to it captures crashes before the service control dispatcher takes over (missing `pywin32`, moved venv, corrupt install). To turn on debug logging without a reinstall, add `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` to the env file the service loads and restart the service.

pages.title: Configure run detection and uploads
pages.description: Choose how the watcher groups files into runs, when files are ready to upload, and whether uploads are automatic or approved.
pages.markdown:
# Configure run detection and uploads (/docs/configure-run-detection)



**For:** Lab operators

Tune three behaviors that decide what becomes a run and when bytes leave the instrument PC: run detection, stability period, and upload mode. Field-by-field schema lives in [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference); this page is the intent guide.

Change these during `data-hub-watcher init`, with `data-hub-watcher config edit`, or by editing `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` then syncing.

## Group files into runs [#group-files-into-runs]

A **run** is one acquisition: a logical group of files the watcher reports together. **Run detection** maps each file’s path (relative to the watch directory) to a run ID.

Common choices:

* **Prefix from filename**: a regex capture, for example everything before the first underscore so `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`
* **One subdirectory per run**: each folder under the watch directory is its own run, so `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`

Presets and custom regex options are listed under [Run detection](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection). Set `recursive: true` when files live in subfolders; otherwise only the top level is watched.

When a run gathers files from several folders, two files can share a name, such as a `run.json` in each capture folder. Watcher 1.1.0 and later keep every copy and add a short tag to the later names, such as `sample~3f9a1c2b.tif`. Older watchers kept only the first; see [Files with the same name were skipped](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#files-with-the-same-name-were-skipped).

If files appear on disk but never become runs, check for `pattern_mismatch` events on the watcher detail page and run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run`.

## Wait until writes finish [#wait-until-writes-finish]

**Stability period** is how many seconds a file must keep the same size and modification time before the watcher treats it as fully written. Default is 5 seconds (allowed range 1–300). Raise it for instruments that write large files slowly.

A file that keeps changing past `max_stability_wait_seconds` (default 300, or 5 minutes) is abandoned with a `stability_timeout` error event. Raise that cap for instruments whose writes take longer; it must be at least the stability period.

## Choose auto or manual upload [#choose-auto-or-manual-upload]

| Mode       | Behavior                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **auto**   | Upload as soon as a file is detected and stable. With watcher 1.2.1 and later, the watcher also picks up files someone requests with **Upload** on the run page, and retries uploads that a restart cut off. |
| **manual** | Report the run, but wait for server approval before uploading bytes. The watcher checks the upload queue once a minute.                                                                                      |

Use manual mode when someone must approve which files leave the instrument PC. Admins manage the queue from the dashboard; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads).

## Existing files on first setup [#existing-files-on-first-setup]

`initial_scan` controls the backlog already in the watch directory when an environment is first entered:

* **`production` default**: upload the backlog (`full`)
* **`staging` / `preview` default**: record a baseline and skip existing files (`new-only`)

Override in config when you need the other behavior. Details: [Initial scan](/docs/configuration-reference#initial-scan).

pages.title: Manage the watcher fleet
pages.description: Monitor watcher health, deregister watchers, and approve or request uploads from the admin dashboard.
pages.markdown:
# Manage the watcher fleet (/docs/manage-watchers)



**For:** Administrators

The **Watchers** area is the fleet view: every registered watcher, its health, deregistration, and the upload queue. Cutting releases and advertising versions is separate: [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

## Monitor watcher health [#monitor-watcher-health]

Each watcher sends a [heartbeat](/docs/concepts#heartbeat) every 60 seconds with version, instrument, watch directory, upload mode, activity counters, and uptime. The fleet list surfaces:

* **Status**: **Online**, **Unresponsive** (no heartbeat for more than 5 minutes), **Stopped** (shut down cleanly), or **Registered** (no first heartbeat yet). See [Watcher status](/docs/concepts#watcher-status).
* **Last heartbeat**: a stale value is the first sign of a stopped, disconnected, or crashed watcher
* **Hostname and instrument assignment**
* **Events**: per-watcher log (`watcher_started`, `run_reported`, `file_uploaded`, `update_*`, and `error` with a `details.kind` discriminator)

Events are the primary remote-diagnosis tool. For operator-side symptoms, see [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

## Deregister a watcher [#deregister-a-watcher]

Each instrument can have at most one active watcher. Deregister the old one when a PC is reimaged or replaced, or to clear “instrument already has an active watcher” on a new install.

* **Web app**: open the watcher under **Watchers** and click **Deregister**, or choose **Deregister** from the watcher’s row menu
* **API**: `DELETE /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId` (requires `watchers:admin`)

Deregistration is a soft-delete: heartbeats, events, and runs stay under **Watchers → Deregistered**. A watcher removed through the API with a token shows that token’s name as the one that removed it.

Retiring an instrument also deregisters its watchers automatically; see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument).

You don’t need to deregister a watcher just because its token was revoked. Re-running `data-hub-watcher init` with a new token takes over the existing registration; see [After revoking a token](/docs/manage-tokens#after-revoking-a-token).

## Request uploads [#request-uploads]

**Upload** on a run page, or on selected runs in a run list, asks the watcher to send files that are still on the instrument PC. The watcher polls the server’s upload queue once a minute and uploads the files that were requested.

* In **manual** upload mode, every file waits in this queue until someone requests it.
* In **auto** upload mode, files upload on their own, and the queue covers files that need another try. This works with watcher 1.2.1 and later; older watchers in auto mode never pick up requests, so the file shows **Uploading** and stays that way.

## Approving manual uploads [#approving-manual-uploads]

For instruments in [manual upload mode](/docs/concepts#upload-mode), the watcher reports runs but waits for server approval before uploading file bytes. Approve a file with **Upload**, or choose **Dismiss** to tell the watcher not to upload it.

Safeguards that keep the queue healthy:

* Changing an instrument’s `watch_directory` reverts pending upload requests to `detected` so stale paths drain instead of erroring
* A queued file that keeps failing (missing on disk or failing to upload) is retried on at most three polls, then cancelled server-side

pages.title: Roll out watcher releases
pages.description: Publish watcher versions to PyPI, advertise them per environment, set a minimum version, force mandatory updates, roll the fleet back, and see what each version adds.
pages.markdown: # Roll out watcher releases (/docs/watcher-releases) **For:** Administrators Lab PCs upgrade themselves toward the version you advertise per environment. You control that from **Settings → Watchers**. How an individual PC installs or runs `self-update` is in [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher). ## How fleet upgrades reach a PC [#how-fleet-upgrades-reach-a-pc] The in-process updater runs from the heartbeat tick on every platform (not only Windows services). Roughly once an hour the watcher: 1. Asks the server for the latest version and compares it to its own 2. Upgrades only if a newer version is available, no files have uploaded for several heartbeats, and no run was reported recently (the activity-window guard). Releases flagged **mandatory** skip this guard 3. Installs the new wheel and restarts into it (Windows services restart via failure-actions policy) 4. Emits `update_started`, then `update_succeeded` or `update_failed`, visible on the dashboard Auto-update is disabled in the `preview` environment so pull-request preview deployments cannot push code to lab PCs. ## Cut a new release [#cut-a-new-release] Releases are tag-driven and publish from a `production` commit. Bump the version in `watcher/pyproject.toml` and merge through `staging` to `production`. Tag and push from `production`: ```sh git checkout production && git pull git tag watcher-v1.3.0 && git push origin watcher-v1.3.0 ``` Approve the `pypi` deployment under **Actions → Publish watcher** in GitHub. In **Settings → Watchers**, pick the new version under **Latest version**. The list comes straight from PyPI, so a release shows up as soon as PyPI publishes it. If PyPI can’t be reached, the field accepts a typed version instead. Each environment has its own database, so set `staging` and `production` separately to roll the fleet gradually. Always tag → publish → verify on PyPI → save. Saving **Latest version** before the wheel is live triggers a wave of `update_failed` events across the fleet. ## Release settings [#release-config-fields] | Field | Purpose | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Latest version** | The version watchers upgrade to. Leave it blank to pause self-updates. | | **Minimum supported version** | Optional. A watcher older than this has its heartbeats rejected with `426 Upgrade Required`, so it shows as unresponsive until it updates. It still checks for updates every hour, so it upgrades itself as long as **Latest version** is newer. Leave it blank for no minimum. | | **Mandatory update** | Skips the activity-window guard; see below. Has no effect while **Latest version** is blank. | ## Mandatory updates [#mandatory-updates] Toggling **Mandatory update** skips the activity-window guard and fires the upgrade on the next hourly check. The server still compares the running version to **Latest version**, so a correctly pinned PC is not forced past its pin. Use sparingly: a forced upgrade mid-acquisition can lose data. Reserve it for security fixes, wire-protocol breaks, or cases where leaving the bad version running is worse than restarting in flight. ## Roll back [#roll-back] Rollback is another release: set **Latest version** back to the older tag for the affected environment(s), turn **Mandatory update** on if you need to bypass the activity-window guard, and wait for the next hourly tick. Turn **Mandatory update** off once the fleet converges. The older wheel remains on PyPI; it is no longer advertised. If **Minimum supported version** is set above the version you roll back to, lower it first. Otherwise the rolled-back watchers can’t check in. ## What each version adds [#what-each-version-adds] Some Data Hub features need a minimum watcher version. Set **Latest version** to at least the version below to turn a feature on across the fleet. | Version | What it adds | | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1.2.1 | **Request upload** works on instruments that upload automatically; older watchers in auto mode leave the file showing **Uploading**. The watcher also retries an automatic upload that didn’t finish, such as one cut off by a restart or an update, the next time it starts. It tries on up to three starts. | | 1.2.0 | Files of 100 MB or more upload in 64 MB parts, and a failed part is retried on its own. Files larger than 5 GB can upload; older watchers are refused for files that large. | | 1.1.0 | When a run gathers files from several folders, files with the same name are all kept instead of only the first. Later copies get a short tag in the name, such as `sample~3f9a1c2b.tif`. Adds the `data-hub-watcher state forget` command. | After upgrading to 1.1.0 or later, files that an older watcher skipped because of a duplicate name aren’t uploaded on their own. To upload them, stop the watcher, run `data-hub-watcher state forget --prefix your_folder_name/` on the instrument PC, and start the watcher again. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#files-with-the-same-name-were-skipped). ## Operator-side failures [#operator-side-failures] If `update_started` is followed by `update_failed`, or auto-update never fires, point operators at [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#auto-update-never-fires) and [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update).

pages.title: Troubleshoot a watcher
pages.description: Fix watcher problems by symptom: will not start, files not detected, uploads stuck, auto-update quiet, and where to find logs.
pages.markdown:
# Troubleshoot a watcher (/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher)



**For:** Lab operators and admins

Find your symptom below. When you are stuck, the [logs](#where-are-the-logs) are the fastest way in. Admins can also inspect heartbeats and events under **Watchers** in the web app.

## Setup and registration [#setup-and-registration]

### “Instrument is still pending activation” [#instrument-is-still-pending-activation]

The instrument was registered but an admin has not confirmed it. Ask an admin to open **Instruments** and click **Confirm**. See [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments).

### “Instrument already has an active watcher” [#instrument-already-has-an-active-watcher]

Each instrument can have at most one active watcher. An earlier install (often on another PC, or before a reimage) is still registered. The CLI prints the existing watcher id; deregister it before re-running `init`:

* **Web app**: **Watchers**, open the existing watcher, click **Deregister**
* **API**: `DELETE /api/v1/watchers/<existing_watcher_id>` with a bearer token that has `watchers:admin`

Deregistration is a soft-delete: history stays under **Watchers → Deregistered**.

### `init` rejects my API key [#init-rejects-my-api-key]

The wizard rejects values that do not start with `dhub_`, and strips zero-width and non-breaking-space characters that Windows clipboards inject. If a paste keeps failing, pass `--show-key` so you can see what the prompt received.

## The watcher will not start [#the-watcher-will-not-start]

* Run `data-hub-watcher config show` to confirm config and environment
* Run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run`: it prints the first failing check
* Confirm the instrument is `active`, not `pending`
* On Windows, if the **service** will not start, see [Windows service](#windows-service)

## The watcher shows Offline right after a restart [#the-watcher-shows-offline-right-after-a-restart]

The watcher checks in once a minute, so a watcher that was just restarted can take up to a minute to show as **Online**. Refresh the page after a minute. If it still shows **Offline** or **Unresponsive**, check that the process is running and see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out).

## Heartbeats fail with `426 Upgrade Required` [#heartbeats-fail-with-426-upgrade-required]

The watcher is older than the **Minimum supported version** an admin set under **Settings → Watchers**, so the server rejects its heartbeats and it shows as unresponsive. It keeps checking for updates every hour and upgrades itself if **Latest version** is newer. To upgrade now, run `data-hub-watcher self-update`. See [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#release-config-fields).

## “Connection error” or “Request timed out” [#connection-error-or-request-timed-out]

The watcher cannot reach the Data Hub API. Check:

* Network connectivity from the instrument PC
* Environment in config (`staging`, `production`, or `preview`): `data-hub-watcher config show`
* That the API base URL for that environment is reachable

## Files are not being detected [#files-are-not-being-detected]

* Confirm the watch directory and file patterns. The instrument’s page in the web app shows both, or run `data-hub-watcher config show` on the PC
* Check that the instrument saves its files into that folder, not a shared network drive or another folder
* Check file patterns. Globs are case-sensitive on some systems (`*.csv` does not match `data.CSV`)
* If files live in subfolders, set run detection to recursive; see [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection)
* Run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run` to preview matches
* Look for `pattern_mismatch` events on the dashboard

## Files are detected but not uploading [#files-are-detected-but-not-uploading]

* In **manual** mode, files wait for approval in the upload queue; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads)
* Check the log for `upload_failed`
* A revoked or expired token surfaces as `401 Unauthorized`. Create a new token and re-run `init`; see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens#after-revoking-a-token)

### A requested upload stays on Uploading [#a-requested-upload-stays-on-uploading]

On an instrument in **auto** mode, **Request upload** needs watcher 1.2.1 or later. Older watchers in auto mode never read the upload queue, so the file shows **Uploading** and never arrives. Update the watcher; see [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds).

### Files larger than 5 GB don’t upload [#files-larger-than-5-gb-dont-upload]

Watchers older than 1.2.0 can’t upload files larger than 5 GB, and Data Hub refuses the upload instead of letting it fail partway. Update the watcher to 1.2.0 or later, which uploads large files in parts.

### An upload was cut off by a restart or an update [#an-upload-was-cut-off-by-a-restart-or-an-update]

Watcher 1.2.1 and later retry an automatic upload that didn’t finish the next time the watcher starts, on up to three starts. Two events tell you when it stops trying:

* `upload_retries_exhausted`: the upload still failed after three starts. Choose **Upload** on the file’s run page to try again.
* `pending_upload_missing`: the file was no longer on disk when the watcher started, so there was nothing to retry.

Older watchers don’t retry; use **Upload** on the run page instead.

### Files with the same name were skipped [#files-with-the-same-name-were-skipped]

When a run gathers files from several folders, watchers older than 1.1.0 uploaded only the first file with a given name and skipped the rest. Watcher 1.1.0 and later keep every copy, adding a short tag to later names. To upload files an older watcher skipped:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Update the watcher to 1.1.0 or later.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Stop the watcher (`data-hub-watcher service stop`, or `Ctrl+C` in the foreground).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Run `data-hub-watcher state forget --prefix your_folder_name/` on the instrument PC, where `your_folder_name/` is the folder under the watch directory that held the skipped files.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Start the watcher again. It reports the files in that folder again and uploads the ones Data Hub doesn’t have.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Auto-update never fires [#auto-update-never-fires]

Check, in order:

* Prefer a long-running service (or scheduled) install; a one-off console session may not stay up for the hourly tick
* Environment is not `preview`: auto-update is hard-disabled there
* Activity-window guard is not holding it up: run `data-hub-watcher self-update`, or ask an admin to flag the release **mandatory**
* **Last Heartbeat** on the dashboard is recent; a stale watcher is not ticking

Upgrade failure modes (`update_started` → `update_failed`, editable installs, missing Scheduled Task) are covered in [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update) and [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

## Windows service [#windows-service]

### The service exits immediately [#the-service-exits-immediately]

If it stops before writing to `watcher.log`:

* Check `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\service-bootstrap.log` for a pre-dispatcher crash (missing `pywin32`, moved venv, corrupt install)
* Query the Windows Application event log:

```powershell
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} |
  Where-Object { $_.ProviderName -match 'Python|DataHubWatcher' -or $_.Message -match 'DataHubWatcher' } |
  Format-List TimeCreated, ProviderName, Id, LevelDisplayName, Message
```

* Run the service in the foreground to see the traceback:

```powershell
& "C:\path\to\venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m win32serviceutil debug DataHubWatcher
```

### `self-update` says “Upgrade dispatched” but nothing happens [#self-update-says-upgrade-dispatched-but-nothing-happens]

On Windows uv-tool installs, the upgrade runs out of process under SYSTEM and takes 30–60s. Track it:

```powershell
Get-Service data-hub-watcher
Get-Content ~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log -Tail 20 -Wait
```

### Turn on debug logging for the service [#turn-on-debug-logging-for-the-service]

Add `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` to the env file the service loads (typically `~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>`) and restart the service. No reinstall needed.

## Where are the logs? [#where-are-the-logs]

Rotating logs (10 MB each, 5 backups). CLI `watch` and the Windows service share one file:

| Platform      | Log file                                    |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Windows       | `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log` |
| macOS / Linux | `~/.data-hub/watcher.log`                   |

Add `--verbose` for debug console output: `data-hub-watcher --verbose watch`. Windows uv-tool upgrade output lands in `~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log`.

## API clients get `401 Unauthorized` [#api-clients-get-401-unauthorized]

The bearer token is missing, mistyped, revoked, or expired. Check **Settings → Access Tokens** and re-issue if needed. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

A script that calls the watcher or processing routes with a browser session, instead of a token, also gets `401`. Those routes accept only personal access tokens; see [How a token acts](/docs/manage-tokens#how-a-token-acts).

## MCP clients get `401 Unauthorized` [#mcp-clients-get-401-unauthorized]

MCP doesn’t accept personal access tokens, so a client configured with `Authorization: Bearer dhub_…` gets a 401 on every call. Remove the header, leave only the URL, and let the client run its sign-in flow. Setup per client is in [MCP overview](/docs/mcp#connect-a-client).

An already-connected client that starts failing has usually lost its grant: sign in again from the client. If reads work and one tool fails with a missing-scope message, the client holds `read` but not `write`; reconnect and approve both.

## Ask an agent to diagnose it [#ask-an-agent-to-diagnose-it]

Use the `troubleshoot_instrument` MCP prompt under [MCP prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts).

pages.markdown: # Manage instruments (/docs/manage-instruments) **For:** Administrators When a lab operator registers an instrument from the watcher, it appears as `pending` and cannot upload until you confirm it. Operator-side setup is in [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). Retiring and reactivating are in [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument). ## Instrument states [#instrument-states] The **Instruments** page has tabs for active, pending, and retired instruments. | Status | UI label | Meaning | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | `pending` | Pending | Registered but not confirmed. Watchers cannot upload. | | `active` | Active | Confirmed and accepting uploads. | | `inactive` | Retired | Deactivated; no new uploads. Historical runs stay browsable. | ## Confirm a pending instrument [#confirm-a-pending-instrument] Open the Data Hub web app and go to **Instruments**. Open the **Pending** tab (or find the yellow `pending` badge). Click **Confirm**. Status becomes `active` and the operator’s watcher can upload. Confirming is admin-only for signed-in users. Under the hood it is `PATCH /api/v1/instruments/:id`. Token automation uses the `instruments:write` scope instead. See the [generated API docs](/docs/api). ## Read an instrument’s page [#view-instrument-health] The top of each instrument page shows what you need to tell whether its files will reach Data Hub: * **Watcher status**: a badge next to the instrument name. **Online** means the watcher checked in recently, **Offline** means it hasn’t, and **No Watcher** means none has registered. The watcher checks in once a minute, so a watcher that was just restarted can take up to a minute to show as online. Hover over the badge for details. * **Watched folder**: the folder the watcher reads from. Hover over it to see which PC it is on. * **File patterns**: the patterns the watcher uploads, such as `*.csv`. Files saved anywhere other than the watched folder, such as a shared network drive, don’t appear in Data Hub. Neither do files whose names don’t match a pattern. The folder and patterns come from the watcher’s config on the instrument PC, so change them there with `data-hub-watcher config edit`; see [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference). Watcher health comes from heartbeats; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers). ## Edit an instrument [#edit-an-instrument] The three-dot menu on an instrument page, and the row menu on the instruments table, hold the admin actions: * **Edit details**: change the **Display name** and the **Instrument type** * **View watcher**: open the watcher registered for this instrument * **Retire** or **Reactivate**: see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument) The instrument type decides which processor reads the instrument’s files, including DishCam and Aunty; see [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). The instrument ID never changes, because it is the storage key prefix.

pages.markdown:
# Retire an instrument (/docs/retire-an-instrument)



**For:** Administrators

Retire an instrument when it is decommissioned or out of service for a long stretch. Retirement sets status to `inactive` (shown as **Retired**), removes it from the sidebar and dashboard lists of live instruments, and stops new uploads. Nothing is deleted from storage; you can reactivate later.

## What retirement does [#what-retirement-does]

When you retire an instrument:

* Status becomes `inactive` (UI: **Retired**), with `retiredAt` / `retiredBy` audit fields
* It stops accepting new runs and watchers
* All existing runs and files stay browsable
* Every active watcher on that instrument is deregistered in the same request so they stop heartbeating

Instrument IDs stay permanent. Retire rather than trying to rename or delete an instrument that has already produced data.

## Retire from the web app [#retire-from-the-web-app]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Open the instrument’s detail page.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Open the admin actions menu and choose **Retire**.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Confirm in the dialog. The dialog lists run count and how many watchers will be deregistered.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The instrument moves to the **Retired** tab on **Instruments**.

## Reactivate [#reactivate]

From a retired instrument’s detail page, choose **Reactivate**. Status returns to `active` and the instrument reappears in the sidebar and dashboard.

Watchers deregistered at retirement do **not** reconnect automatically. An operator must re-register (usually `data-hub-watcher init` on the instrument PC) after reactivation.

## Via the API [#via-the-api]

```sh
# Retire
curl -X PATCH https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments/bio-rad-cfx96 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status":"inactive"}'

# Reactivate
curl -X PATCH https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments/bio-rad-cfx96 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status":"active"}'
```

Session callers need the admin role; bearer tokens need `instruments:write`.

pages.markdown:
# Issue and revoke tokens (/docs/manage-tokens)



**For:** Administrators

Personal access tokens authenticate the watcher, the processing Lambda, and scripts that call the Data Hub API. Creating and revoking tokens requires the workspace admin role. Members can view the list at **Settings → Access Tokens** but cannot create or delete tokens. Roles and scopes: [Security and permissions](/docs/security).

## How a token acts [#how-a-token-acts]

A token acts as itself, under its own name. It doesn’t act as the admin who created it or as any other person.

* Anything a token does is recorded under the token’s name: comments, deleting a run, retiring an instrument, removing a watcher, and notifications sent through the API.
* Run pages, instrument pages, watcher pages, comments, and the notification bell show the token’s name with a key icon.
* A token can post comments, and it can edit and delete only the comments it posted.

Some actions need a signed-in person, so tokens can’t do them at all: claiming runs, sending feedback, and reviewing feedback. AI assistants aren’t affected, because they sign in as the person who approved them; see [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

The reverse also holds: the API routes that the watcher and the Lambda call accept only tokens. A browser session gets `401 Unauthorized` on watcher registration and heartbeats, upload links, file updates, run creation and updates, and instrument creation.

## Create a token [#create-a-token]

### In the web app [#in-the-web-app]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Sign in as an admin.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Go to **Settings → Access Tokens**.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Click **Create token**.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Enter a **Name** that identifies the client (for example, `FPLC watcher, Lab 201`). This is the name people see wherever the token acts, so make it recognizable.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Pick an **Expiration**: 30 days, 90 days (the default), 1 year, or no expiry.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Under **Scopes**, click a preset, or click **Customize scopes** to pick individual scopes.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Click **Create token**.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The plaintext token is shown once: copy it immediately. It starts with `dhub_` followed by a 64-character hex string.

### Scope presets [#scope-presets]

A preset selects the minimum scopes a common client needs:

* **Read-only**: view instruments, runs, files, watchers, and archive jobs; change nothing
* **Watcher**: what a watcher needs to register, report runs, and upload files
* **Lambda**: what the processing Lambda needs to read instruments and runs, and write run and file results

<Callout type="info">
  The **Lambda** preset includes `runs:read`, which DishCam processing needs to pair each photo stack with its `run.json`. A Lambda token created from an older preset gets `403 FORBIDDEN` on DishCam files. Create a new token from the current preset and update the Lambda’s `DATA_HUB_API_KEY`; the [Lambda developer docs](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#supported-instrument-types) describe the swap.
</Callout>

You cannot change a token’s scopes after creation. To change them, revoke the token and create a new one.

### Via the API [#via-the-api]

Creating and deleting tokens is admin-only and needs a signed-in browser session (cookie). Tokens cannot manage other tokens.

```sh
curl -X POST https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/tokens \
  -H "Cookie: session_cookie_here" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "FPLC watcher",
    "scopes": ["instruments:read", "instruments:write", "watchers:read", "watchers:report", "runs:create", "runs:update", "runs:upload", "files:update"],
    "expires_at": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z"
  }'
```

`scopes` is required and must be a non-empty list of explicit scopes. The wildcard `*` and the older coarse scopes `runs:write`, `files:write`, and `watchers:write` are rejected. `expires_at` is optional; if omitted, the token never expires. The request is rejected if it includes `user_id`, because tokens don’t belong to a person. The response includes the plaintext once in the `token` field.

## Use a token [#use-a-token]

### With the watcher [#with-the-watcher]

During `data-hub-watcher init`, paste the token when prompted. Or set it first:

```sh
export DATA_HUB_API_KEY=dhub_your_token_here
data-hub-watcher init
```

### With the REST API [#with-the-rest-api]

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

More in the [API overview](/docs/api).

Tokens don’t authenticate MCP clients, which sign in with OAuth instead. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

## View tokens [#view-tokens]

**Settings → Access Tokens** lists every active token with these columns:

* **Name**
* **Created by**: the admin who made the token. For tokens created before October 6, 2026, this shows the person the token used to act as.
* **Token**: the prefix only, because the full token is never stored
* **Scopes**
* **Last used**
* **Expires**
* **Created**

## Revoke a token [#revoke-a-token]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Go to **Settings → Access Tokens**.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Click the delete icon on the token’s row and confirm.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The token stops working immediately. Clients using it start receiving `401 Unauthorized`.

```sh
curl -X DELETE https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/tokens/<token_id> \
  -H "Cookie: session_cookie_here"
```

A revoked token leaves the list, but Data Hub keeps its record. Wherever the token acted, its name stays visible and is marked **(revoked)**.

## After revoking a token [#after-revoking-a-token]

If a running watcher used that token:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Create a new token with the **Watcher** preset.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    On the instrument PC, re-run `data-hub-watcher init` and enter the new token. The new token takes over the existing watcher registration, so you don’t need to deregister the old one first.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Restart the watcher (`data-hub-watcher watch` or the Windows service).
  </Step>
</Steps>

## When someone leaves [#when-someone-leaves]

Tokens keep working after the admin who created them leaves or their account is deleted, because tokens act as themselves. When someone leaves, check the **Created by** column and revoke any of their tokens that nobody else should keep using.

## Token hygiene [#token-hygiene]

* Name tokens so you can tell which PC or client each belongs to
* Set expirations for temporary setups
* Scope to least privilege; see [Token scopes](/docs/security#token-scopes)
* Revoke immediately when a watcher is decommissioned or a token may have been exposed

Tokens are hashed with SHA-256 before storage; plaintext is never persisted.

pages.description: Promote and demote workspace admins from Settings → Members.
pages.markdown: # Manage members (/docs/manage-members) **For:** Administrators Workspace members sign in with Google OAuth. Admins decide who else has the admin role. Member vs admin capabilities are summarized in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles). ## Open the members list [#open-the-members-list] Go to **Settings → Members**. Non-admins who open the URL see an “Admins only” message; the settings sidebar hides the entry for them. The table lists every signed-in user: name, email, role badge, and an **Admin** toggle. ## Promote or demote [#promote-or-demote] Toggle **Admin** on a row to grant or revoke admin access. Every privileged action re-checks the database, so the change applies to that user’s next one. Their view of the dashboard can lag by up to 5 minutes, because admin-only buttons and sidebar entries come from their [cached session](/docs/security#session-lifetime). You cannot demote yourself. That guard prevents locking the workspace out of its last admin. Ask another admin to demote you if needed. ## First admin bootstrap [#first-admin-bootstrap] The first admins come from the `ADMIN_EMAILS` environment variable (comma-separated, case-insensitive). Listed users are promoted on every sign-in. After that, any admin can promote others from this page. There is no invite flow in the product: people appear here after they sign in successfully to your deployment. Every Google account your OAuth client accepts can sign in, so that client, not this page, controls who appears here. See [Who can sign in](/docs/security#who-can-sign-in).

pages.title: Set up integrations
pages.description: Connect Data Hub to Linear for feedback reports, and to Slack for personal direct messages and a shared new-run channel, from Settings → Integrations.
pages.markdown:
# Set up integrations (/docs/integrations)



**For:** Administrators and engineers

**Settings → Integrations** holds the connections the whole workspace shares. Only admins see it. The page has three parts:

* **Linear**: where feedback reports go, and where their status comes from
* **Slack app**: the credentials behind personal Slack direct messages and **Connect to Slack**
* **Slack channel**: a webhook that posts a message to a shared channel whenever a new run arrives

Each person’s own notification choices are separate, under **Settings → Notifications**. See [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications).

## How secrets are stored [#integration-secrets-key]

Data Hub encrypts the secrets you paste on this page before saving them: the Linear client secret and signing secret, and the Slack bot token and client secret. It never shows a saved secret again. To change one, paste a new value and save.

Encryption needs the `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` environment variable on the web app. It is 64 hexadecimal characters; generate one with `openssl rand -hex 32`, set it in Vercel, and redeploy. Until it is set, saving a secret fails, and the Slack app card says so.

If the key changes after secrets were saved, Data Hub can’t read them anymore. The affected field says **Can’t read saved value**. Put the old key back, or paste the value again and save.

## Linear for feedback reports [#linear]

Feedback that people send from Data Hub becomes an issue in your Linear workspace, and the report’s status follows that issue. Until an admin saves a Linear team here, the **Feedback** item stays out of the account menu, and sending feedback through the API or an AI assistant returns an error saying feedback isn’t set up. What reporters see is in [Send feedback](/docs/send-feedback).

The Linear card walks you through four steps.

### 1. Connect your Linear app [#linear-connect]

Data Hub signs in to Linear as an app, so you create one app in Linear for it.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    In Linear, go to **Settings → API → OAuth applications** and create a new application.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Name it **Data Hub**. Linear shows this name on every issue it files.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Linear asks for a callback URL. Data Hub doesn’t use one, so paste the URL shown in the step, which is your deployment’s address.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Turn on **Client credentials**, then save.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Copy the client ID and client secret into the Linear card in Data Hub, and choose **Connect**.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Data Hub checks the credentials with Linear before it saves them. If client credentials are turned off for the app, the card says so; turn them on in the app’s settings in Linear and choose **Connect** again.

If the credentials belong to a different Linear workspace than the one already connected, Data Hub asks before switching. Switching clears the team, project, labels, and signing secret. Issues already in Linear stay there.

### 2. Choose where reports go [#linear-destination]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Pick the **Team** that receives reports. Only public teams are listed, because Linear doesn’t show private teams to apps.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Optionally pick a **Project**.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Optionally pick a label for each kind of report: **Bug**, **Feature request**, and **Other**. Labels can come from the team or from the whole workspace. Linear adds the matching label to each new issue.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Choose **Save and turn on feedback**. Everyone sees **Feedback** in their account menu from then on.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Changing the team later clears the project and labels. Status updates also stop until the Linear webhook from step 3 points at the new team.

### 3. Get status updates from Linear [#linear-status-updates]

A webhook tells Data Hub when an issue changes, so it can update the report and tell the person who sent it when the issue closes.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    In Linear, go to **Settings → API** and choose **New webhook**.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Paste the **Webhook URL** shown in the step. It ends in `/api/v1/integrations/linear/webhook`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    For **Team**, choose the team from step 2. Under events, turn on **Issues** only.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Save the webhook, then copy its signing secret into **Signing secret** in Data Hub and save.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Data Hub uses the signing secret to check that each update really comes from Linear. The step shows **Waiting for an update from Linear** until the first one arrives. Any change to an issue in the team sends one, including the test report in the next step.

### 4. Send a test report [#linear-test-report]

Choose **Send test report**. Data Hub files a report as you and links to the new Linear issue. Move that issue to **Done** in Linear. The step confirms that the issue closed and that you got a Data Hub notification. You can also skip the test.

### After setup [#linear-after-setup]

Once setup is finished, the Linear card shows a summary: the connected workspace, where reports go, whether status updates are working and when the last one arrived, and what reporters see for each Linear status.

| When the Linear issue moves to          | The reporter sees |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| **Done**, or any other completed status | Resolved          |
| **Canceled**                            | Declined          |
| **Duplicate**                           | Declined          |
| Any other status                        | Open              |

Data Hub notifies the reporter once, when the issue first closes. Moving an issue from one closed status to another, such as **Done** to **Released**, doesn’t notify again. Reopening an issue and closing it again does.

If Data Hub keeps rejecting updates from Linear, **Status updates** shows **Not working**. The usual cause is a wrong signing secret, or Linear turning the webhook off after repeated failures. Paste the signing secret again from the webhook’s page in Linear, and check that the webhook is still turned on.

**Disconnect Linear** turns feedback off. Issues already in Linear stay there.

## Slack app for direct messages [#slack-app]

Personal Slack direct messages and the **Connect to Slack** button use one shared Slack app. Create the app once in the [Slack API portal](https://api.slack.com/apps), then give Data Hub its credentials. You can reuse an existing Slack app, including the one behind the channel webhook.

### Create the app [#create-the-slack-app]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    In the Slack API portal, choose **Create New App → From scratch**, or open an existing app.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Under **OAuth & Permissions**, add these scopes:

    **Bot Token Scopes:**

    | Scope        | Purpose                                      |
    | ------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
    | `chat:write` | Send direct messages with `chat.postMessage` |

    **User Token Scopes:**

    | Scope     | Purpose                             |
    | --------- | ----------------------------------- |
    | `openid`  | Sign in with Slack (OpenID Connect) |
    | `profile` | Display name in the identity token  |
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Under **Redirect URLs**, add one callback URL per environment. The path is always `/api/v1/settings/slack/callback`:

    | Environment | Example URL                                                          |
    | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    | Local       | `http://localhost:3000/api/v1/settings/slack/callback`               |
    | Staging     | `https://staging.datahub.example.com/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` |
    | Production  | `https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/settings/slack/callback`         |

    `SLACK_REDIRECT_URI`, or the request origin plus that path when unset, must match a listed URL exactly.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Under **Install App**, choose **Install to Workspace** (or **Reinstall** after changing scopes).
  </Step>
</Steps>

### Give Data Hub the credentials [#slack-app-credentials]

Enter the credentials in the **Slack app** card under **Settings → Integrations**, or set them as environment variables on the web app. A value saved in the card takes effect right away, with no redeploy, and is used instead of the matching environment variable.

| Card field               | Environment variable  | Where to find it                                        | Required                                                  |
| ------------------------ | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bot token**            | `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`     | **Install App** → Bot User OAuth Token (`xoxb-…`)       | Yes                                                       |
| **Client ID**            | `SLACK_CLIENT_ID`     | **Basic Information** → App Credentials                 | Yes                                                       |
| **Client secret**        | `SLACK_CLIENT_SECRET` | **Basic Information** → App Credentials                 | Yes                                                       |
| **Allowed workspace ID** | `SLACK_TEAM_ID`       | Workspace URL segment `T…` in `app.slack.com/client/T…` | No, but recommended so connections stay on your workspace |

Each field shows where its value comes from: **Saved here**, **Using** followed by the variable name, or **Not set**. **Remove saved value** makes the environment variable the source again. If Data Hub can’t read a saved value, for example because `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` changed, it uses the environment variable in the meantime.

Two settings exist only as environment variables, and changing them needs a redeploy:

| Variable             | Purpose                                                                                                            | Required                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| `SLACK_STATE_SECRET` | Signs the short-lived value Data Hub checks while a person connects Slack. Generate with `openssl rand -base64 32` | No (falls back to `AUTH_SECRET`) |
| `SLACK_REDIRECT_URI` | Full callback URL, when it differs from the request origin                                                         | No                               |

Members can then connect under **Settings → Notifications**. Deploy runbooks are linked from [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting).

## Slack channel for new runs [#slack-channel]

The **Slack channel** card holds a Slack incoming webhook. Data Hub posts one message to that channel each time a new run is reported. This is separate from personal direct messages, which each person turns on for themselves.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    In your Slack app, open **Incoming Webhooks**, turn them on, and add a webhook for the channel you want.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Copy the webhook URL. It starts with `https://hooks.slack.com/services/`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Paste it into the **Slack channel** card and save. The card shows **Configured** and who last changed it.
  </Step>
</Steps>

To change channels, paste a new webhook URL. To stop the messages, remove the webhook. This setting has no environment variable.

pages.markdown:
# Overview (/docs/api)



**For:** Developers and integrators

The Data Hub API is served by the web application at `/api/v1/`. The watcher, Lambda, and dashboard all call it. Data Hub is self-hosted, so the base URL is your deployment host plus `/api/v1`. Examples use `https://datahub.example.com`; substitute your host.

Per-endpoint request and response shapes live in the generated pages under this section (same sidebar). Each deployment also publishes OpenAPI 3.1 at `/api/v1/openapi.json`.

## Authentication [#authentication]

Two methods (full model in [Security and permissions](/docs/security)):

* **Session cookies**: web dashboard (Google OAuth). Session callers implicitly hold every scope.
* **Bearer tokens**: `Authorization: Bearer dhub_…` for the watcher, the Lambda, and scripts

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

Every token request needs a [scope](/docs/security#token-scopes). A missing scope returns `403 FORBIDDEN`. Some mutations also require the admin role; see [Admin-gated operations](/docs/security#admin-gated-operations).

Some routes accept only one of the two methods:

* The routes the watcher and the Lambda call accept only tokens, and return `401 UNAUTHORIZED` to a session. These cover watcher registration and heartbeats, upload links, file updates, run creation and updates, and instrument creation.
* Claiming runs, sending feedback, reviewing feedback, and managing tokens need a signed-in person, so tokens can’t call them.

Mint tokens in the UI: [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

## First request [#first-request]

List instruments:

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

Fetch the OpenAPI document (no auth required):

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/openapi.json
```

The document covers the integrator surface: instruments, runs, comments, files, watchers, archive jobs, search, and `POST /notifications/dispatch`. Routes that only the dashboard uses are left out: `/tokens`, `/users`, `/feedback`, `/settings/*`, and the notification inbox. The MCP transport is documented separately.

## Actions taken by a token [#actions-taken-by-a-token]

A token acts under its own name, not as a person, so responses name the token when it did something:

* A comment posted by a token has `user: null` and a `token` object with the token’s `id` and `name`. A comment posted by a person has `token: null`.
* A run deleted by a token has `deleted_by_token` set, alongside `deleted_at`.

Read both fields when you display who did something. See [How a token acts](/docs/manage-tokens#how-a-token-acts).

## Send notifications [#send-notifications]

`POST /notifications/dispatch` sends a short message to chosen people, with an optional link to a run. It needs a token with the `notifications:create` scope. Each person’s **Service notifications** setting decides whether the message appears in the notification bell, as a Slack direct message, or both. The message shows the token’s name as its sender. Request fields are on the generated [dispatch notifications](/docs/api/notifications/dispatchNotifications) page.

## Pagination and filtering [#pagination-and-filtering]

List endpoints that return pages (notably run search) accept:

* `page`: 1-based page index
* `per_page`: page size, 1 to 100

Responses include pagination metadata such as `page`, `per_page`, `total`, and `total_pages`.

Run report items page by index instead, with `offset` and `limit` (max 200). Their responses return `offset`, `limit`, and `total`.

Run search also supports filters (instrument, date range, attribution via `ranBy`, and instrument-specific metadata). Exact query parameters are on each generated operation page in the sidebar under this **API** section.

## Error responses [#error-responses]

Errors use a nested envelope:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Instrument not found.",
    "details": null
  }
}
```

Common codes: `VALIDATION_ERROR` (400), `UNAUTHORIZED` (401), `FORBIDDEN` (403), `NOT_FOUND` (404), `CONFLICT` (409). Scope failures use `code: "FORBIDDEN"` with a message naming the missing scope.

Feedback routes have two more. `LINEAR_UNAVAILABLE` (502) means Data Hub couldn’t reach Linear, where reports are stored. `FEEDBACK_NOT_CONFIGURED` (503) means no admin has connected Linear yet; see [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations#linear).

## MCP [#mcp]

`GET` and `POST` `/mcp/v1` expose the MCP server over Streamable HTTP, outside the `/api/v1` tree. Clients authenticate with OAuth rather than a personal access token, and hold `read` to connect plus `write` to call any tool that changes data. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

pages.markdown:
# Overview (/docs/mcp)



**For:** Developers and integrators

Data Hub exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `/mcp/v1` so AI clients can query instruments, runs, files, and watcher health. Clients authenticate by sending you through a browser sign-in.

Catalogs for [tools](/docs/mcp/tools), [prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts), and [resources](/docs/mcp/resources) are generated from the live server schema, so they match what your client discovers when it connects.

## Authentication [#authentication]

The MCP server authenticates with OAuth. All you need to provide is the endpoint URL; for example, `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1`.

The first connection opens your browser:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Sign in to Data Hub with Google, unless you already have a session open.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Read the **Authorize application** screen. It names the client, the host it redirects to, and the access it’s asking for.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    Click **Allow**.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Your client stores the access token it receives and renews it without asking again. **Allow** grants everything on the screen: there are no per-permission checkboxes, so click **Deny** if any line looks wrong.

### Scopes [#scopes]

MCP uses two scopes rather than the `<resource>:<action>` scopes that gate REST requests:

* **`read`**: required to connect at all, and covers every read-only tool, resource, and prompt
* **`write`**: additionally required by tools that change something, including claiming runs, commenting, requesting uploads, reprocessing, and deleting

Most clients ask for both, because the server advertises both. A client granted only `read` still connects and still reads; its first mutating tool call fails with a message naming the missing scope.

Each entry in the [tools catalog](/docs/mcp/tools) lists the scope its REST equivalent requires, which tells you what data the tool touches. Over MCP, only `read` and `write` are enforced.

The client acts as you, with your role. Admin-only actions, such as deleting someone else’s comment, work over MCP only when you are an admin. Claiming runs and sending feedback work because a signed-in person is behind the client, even though API tokens can’t do either.

## Connect a client [#connect-a-client]

Examples use `https://datahub.example.com`; substitute your deployment host.

### Claude Code [#claude-code]

Register the server with [`claude mcp add`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart). Run this in your terminal, not inside a `claude` session:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user data-hub https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1
```

Confirm that the server was added by running `claude mcp list`. Then, start a session with `claude` and run `/mcp` to authenticate.

### Claude Desktop [#claude-desktop]

Remote servers go through **Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector**. The `claude_desktop_config.json` file handles local servers only. Paste `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1` as the URL, click **Add**, then click **Connect** to sign in. Leave the OAuth client fields under **Advanced settings** empty, since Data Hub registers clients on demand.

<Callout type="info">
  Claude reaches your server from Anthropic’s infrastructure rather than from your own machine, so the deployment has to be reachable from the public internet. A deployment running on `localhost` can’t be added this way; use Claude Code or Cursor for local work.
</Callout>

### Cursor [#cursor]

Add the server to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "data-hub": {
      "url": "https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1"
    }
  }
}
```

Open **Settings → Tools & MCP**. The server appears with a **Needs authentication** label; click it to start the browser flow. The tools show up once you approve the grant.

### Other clients [#other-clients]

Any client that speaks Streamable HTTP and the MCP authorization spec needs one setting, the URL `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1`. For local development, point at `http://localhost:3000/mcp/v1` instead.

Clients that speak MCP but not OAuth can bridge through [`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote), which runs the browser flow on their behalf.

## Questions about Data Hub [#questions-about-data-hub]

The assistant can answer questions about Data Hub itself, such as how to install a watcher or what a run status means. It searches the documentation and the [changelog](/docs/send-feedback#changelog), reads the page that fits, and links it in its answer. Two tools do this, and both need only the `read` scope:

* `search_docs` returns up to five matching sections, each with a short excerpt and a link
* `read_doc` returns one page, or one section of a page, as Markdown

The answers come from the docs that ship with your deployment, so they match the version you run, including a staging deployment that is ahead of the published site. Clients that let you attach resources by hand can also attach any page as `datahub://docs/<page>`, for example `datahub://docs/manage-tokens`.

The assistant reads the guides and the changelog. It doesn’t read the generated [API](/docs/api) endpoint pages or the [tools](/docs/mcp/tools), [prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts), and [resources](/docs/mcp/resources) catalogs, because the client already receives the catalog when it connects. When a search finds nothing, the assistant says the docs don’t cover the question and offers to [send feedback](#feedback) about the gap.

## Interactive run reports [#interactive-run-reports]

Clients that support MCP Apps, an extension of the Model Context Protocol, show the same interactive run report as the web app when the assistant calls `get_run_report`. The report includes image carousels, plate maps, and the Aunty plate with its well charts. Clients without MCP Apps support get the same data as text and describe it instead.

## Feedback [#feedback]

The assistant can send [feedback about Data Hub](/docs/send-feedback) for you, for example after a tool call fails. It shows you the draft first and sends it only after you agree. Sending feedback needs only the `read` scope. The assistant can also list the reports you sent and read one in full, by report ID or by Linear issue ID such as `ENG-1476`. Feedback tools return an error saying feedback isn’t set up until an admin [connects Linear](/docs/integrations#linear).

Problems with one run’s data belong in a run comment instead, which the assistant can also post.

## Machine-readable catalog [#machine-readable-catalog]

Fetch the same catalog these pages render from:

```bash
curl https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1/schema.json
```

It lists every tool, prompt, and resource, with JSON Schema for arguments and each tool's response. The schema document needs no authentication.

pages.markdown:
# Concepts (/docs/concepts)



**For:** Everyone

Short definitions of the vocabulary the rest of these docs use. If you’ve arrived mid-page and a term is unfamiliar, it’s defined here. Terms are grouped by what they describe: the equipment, the data, the rules that turn files into runs, and who can do what.

## Equipment and fleet [#equipment-and-fleet]

### Instrument [#instrument]

A piece of lab equipment registered in Data Hub, identified by a kebab-case **instrument ID** (e.g., `akta-fplc`, `bio-rad-cfx96`). The ID is permanent, because it becomes the storage key prefix and the identifier used across the system. A human-readable display name sits alongside it.

An instrument has three states. The dashboard groups instruments into a tab per state and shows connection health separately:

| State      | Shown as                                      | Meaning                                                                      |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pending`  | **Pending** tab                               | Registered but not yet confirmed by an admin. A watcher can’t upload for it. |
| `active`   | **Active** tab, with Online or Offline health | Confirmed and accepting uploads.                                             |
| `inactive` | **Retired** tab                               | Deactivated. No longer accepting uploads, but its runs stay browsable.       |

See [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments), and [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument).

### Instrument type [#instrument-type]

Separate from the instrument ID. The type tells Data Hub which [preprocessor](#preprocessor) to run on files from this instrument, so it controls what metadata, badges, and reports you get.

Admins set it from the instrument page: open the three-dot menu, choose **Edit details**, and pick a supported type. An instrument with no matching type still stores and serves raw files. It gets no extracted metadata and no processed artifacts. See [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing).

### Watcher [#watcher]

The `data-hub-watcher` command-line program that runs on an instrument PC. It monitors a directory, groups new files into runs, uploads them to cloud storage, and reports status to the API. Each instrument can have at most one active watcher at a time.

A watcher is registered with the API and carries one registration ID per [environment](#environment). Deregistering a watcher is a [soft delete](#soft-delete): its history stays visible for auditing. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers).

### Watcher status [#watcher-status]

What the **Watchers** page shows for each watcher, derived from its most recent [heartbeat](#heartbeat):

| Status           | Meaning                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Online**       | A heartbeat arrived in the last 5 minutes.                                                                    |
| **Unresponsive** | No heartbeat for more than 5 minutes. The process crashed, the PC is off, or the network is blocking the API. |
| **Stopped**      | The watcher shut down cleanly and said so in its last heartbeat.                                              |
| **Registered**   | The watcher registered but hasn’t sent its first heartbeat yet.                                               |

An unresponsive watcher keeps its registration and history, so you can read its last events to work out what happened. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

Instrument pages and the instruments table sum this up per instrument: **Online** if any of its watchers is online, **Offline** if none is, and **No Watcher** if none has registered.

### Heartbeat [#heartbeat]

A status ping the watcher sends to the API every 60 seconds. It carries the watcher version, instrument ID, watch directory, upload mode, activity counters, and uptime, and it drives the **Last Heartbeat** column and the online health shown on the dashboard. The same tick runs the auto-updater. The upload queue is checked separately, also once a minute, so a slow upload can’t delay a heartbeat.

### Events [#events]

A per-watcher log of lifecycle moments and errors: `watcher_started`, `run_reported`, `file_uploaded`, `update_succeeded`, and `error` (with a `details.kind` discriminator), among others. Events are batched and flushed on each heartbeat and are visible on the dashboard, which makes them the primary tool for diagnosing a watcher remotely. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

### Environment [#environment]

Which Data Hub deployment a watcher talks to: `staging`, `production`, or `preview` (a Vercel preview deployment, which needs an explicit API base URL). Staging and production are separate deployments with separate databases, so a single PC keeps an independent registration and local state per environment and can switch between them.

## Data [#data]

### Run [#run]

A logical grouping of files produced by one acquisition. The watcher assigns each file a **run ID** using its configured [run detection](#run-detection) method, then reports the run to the API. The first file for a run creates it; later files are added incrementally to the same run’s manifest.

### Run status [#run-status]

How far a run’s files have got from the instrument to the dashboard. These are the values you can filter by under **Add filter** on any run list:

| Status         | Meaning                                                                                                      |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Failed         | At least one file stopped on an error. [Reprocess](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-and-delete) after a fix.      |
| Stalled        | At least one file has been processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing. Reprocess it to try again. |
| Pending upload | The watcher found the files but hasn’t sent them yet.                                                        |
| Uploaded       | The files are in storage. Processing hasn’t started, or this instrument type has no preprocessor.            |
| Processing     | The preprocessor is reading the files, extracting metadata, and building reports.                            |
| Completed      | Processing finished.                                                                                         |
| Empty          | The run has no files.                                                                                        |

When a run’s files are in different states, the run shows the first status in this table that applies.

### File and file category [#file-and-file-category]

Every file in a run carries a category, shown as a label in the run’s files table:

* **Raw**: what the instrument wrote, uploaded unchanged
* **Processed**: what a [preprocessor](#preprocessor) generated from a raw file, such as a CSV of well values, a contrast-adjusted PNG, or a preview JPG

Both categories download the same way, and file filters on the run page work on this label. See [Download files](/docs/browse-runs#download-files).

### Preprocessor [#preprocessor]

The server-side code that reads a raw file, extracts metadata, and writes processed files. It runs in an AWS Lambda when a file arrives in raw storage, or when you choose **Reprocess**. Which preprocessor runs depends on the [instrument type](#instrument-type), and not every type has one. Per-type inputs and outputs are in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing).

### Run archive [#run-archive]

The zip that **Download all** builds for a run. It covers the run’s active files and respects any file filter you have applied. Large archives build in the background as an archive job, so the first request can return a wait time rather than a file.

### Attribution [#attribution]

The record of who ran a run. Use **Claim** on the run to attribute yourself. Attribution is self-only: you claim or unclaim your own user, and you can’t attribute someone else. API tokens can’t claim runs. Claims drive **My runs** and the “ran by” filters, and claiming a run subscribes you to its comments. See [Claim who ran it](/docs/browse-runs#claim-who-ran-it).

## Turning files into runs [#turning-files-into-runs]

### Run detection [#run-detection]

The rule that maps a file to a run ID. Two broad strategies:

* **Prefix**: a regex extracts the run ID from the filename. The default `^([^_]+)` takes everything before the first underscore, so `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`
* **Directory**: each subdirectory under the watch directory is its own run, so `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`

The full set of presets, and the custom-regex option, is in the [Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection).

### Stability period [#stability-period]

How many seconds a file must stay unchanged (same size and modification time) before the watcher treats it as fully written and eligible for upload. The default is 5 seconds; raise it for instruments that write large files slowly. A file that keeps changing past `max_stability_wait_seconds` (default 300, or 5 minutes) is abandoned with a `stability_timeout` error event.

### Upload mode [#upload-mode]

How files get from the instrument to cloud storage:

* **auto**: files upload immediately after they’re detected and stabilized. With watcher 1.2.1 and later, the watcher also uploads files someone requests from the run page
* **manual**: runs are reported to the server, but files aren’t uploaded until approved through the server-side upload queue, which the watcher checks once a minute. Use this when uploads need human approval

### Initial scan [#initial-scan]

What the watcher does with files already sitting in the watch directory the first time an environment is entered. `production` uploads the existing backlog (`full`). `staging` and `preview` record it as a baseline and skip it (`new-only`), so test environments aren’t flooded with history. See the [Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference#initial-scan).

### Dismiss [#dismiss]

For instruments in [manual upload mode](#upload-mode), dismissing a detected file tells the watcher not to upload it. Dismissing differs from deleting: the file never reached Data Hub storage, so there’s nothing to restore. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads).

### Soft delete [#soft-delete]

Data Hub marks things deleted rather than erasing them, so history survives for auditing. Deleting a run hides it from run lists without removing its stored files, and **Show deleted runs** brings it back into view. Deregistering a watcher keeps its events and heartbeats. Anyone signed in can restore a deleted run from the run page.

## People and access [#people-and-access]

### Role [#role]

Data Hub has two roles, **Member** and **Admin**. Members sign in, browse instruments and runs, claim and comment on runs, send feedback, and read the token list. Admins can also confirm and update instruments, create and revoke tokens, promote or demote other users, delete any comment, review feedback, and manage integrations. Full permission tables are in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles).

### Personal access token [#personal-access-token]

A `dhub_`-prefixed bearer token that authenticates the watcher, and other API clients, with the Data Hub API. Tokens carry permission [scopes](#scope) and are created and revoked by admins. The plaintext is shown once, at creation.

A token acts as itself, under its own name. Comments it posts and runs it deletes show the token’s name with a key icon, not a person. Because a token isn’t a person, it can’t claim runs or send feedback. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

### Scope [#scope]

A permission string carried by a token, such as `runs:read`. A token-authenticated request is refused with `403 FORBIDDEN` when the token’s scopes don’t cover what the route requires. Dashboard sessions hold every scope, so scope checks only apply to token requests. The scope table is in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#token-scopes).

### Feedback report [#feedback-report]

A bug report or feature request about Data Hub itself, sent from the account menu or by an AI assistant. Each report is stored as an issue in your workspace’s Linear, and its status (Open, Resolved, or Declined) follows that issue. See [Send feedback and see what’s new](/docs/send-feedback).
